articles.title: COP17: The world has a plan to save nature. Is it working?
articles.summary: The UN Secretary-General has called for an end to the “war on nature”. On Monday, governments gathering in Yerevan, Armenia, will have to confront a more practical question: are they doing enough to win the peace and put the world’s biodiversity goals back on track?
articles.content:
COP17, the UN Biodiversity Conference, comes at a critical halfway point in the global effort to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030. Running from 19 to 30 October, the meeting will take stock of progress, identify where countries are falling behind and, crucially, consider how to accelerate action over the next four years.

Here’s what you need to know:

First things first: What is the global biodiversity framework?

The big picture: Think of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework as the world’s blueprint for halting and reversing the destruction of nature.

Agreed in 2022, it contains 23 targets for 2030 and four longer-term goals for 2050. It tackles the main drivers of biodiversity loss, including changes in how land and seas are used, unsustainable exploitation of species, climate change, pollution and invasive species.

Its best known ambition is “30 by 30”: conserving 30 per cent of land and sea by 2030, the deadline for achieving the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

But, the framework goes much further, including financing for biodiversity, reforming harmful incentives, encouraging more sustainable production and consumption and addressing businesses’ impacts and dependencies on nature.

So, how are we doing?

Reality check: We’re not moving fast enough.

There has been movement. Nearly 90 per cent of the 196 parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity have established national biodiversity targets, close to 60 per cent have developed national biodiversity strategies and action plans and more than 70 per cent have submitted national reports.

But, fewer than half of the national targets assessed by parties are on track. Ambition also remains short of the 30-by-30 goal, while major gaps persist in finance, capacity, cooperation and the data needed to track progress.

As Secretary-General António Guterres told leaders in Yerevan on Friday: “Halfway to 2030, Yerevan is our moment of accountability.”

What’s actually on the table at COP17?

Why it matters: COP17 is essentially about moving from promises to delivery.

Among the big issues governments will grapple with:

Taking stock: Countries will undertake the first global review of collective progress under the framework, examining what has been achieved since 2022 and where faster action is needed.

Countries will undertake the first global review of collective progress under the framework, examining what has been achieved since 2022 and where faster action is needed. Closing the implementation gap: The question is how to translate national targets and plans into measurable results on the ground.

The question is how to translate national targets and plans into measurable results on the ground. Finding the money: The framework calls for at least $200 billion annually from all sources by 2030 , including at least $30 billion in international biodiversity finance, according to Armenia’s UN Ambassador Paruyr Hovhannisyan.

Making the Cali Fund work: Governments will have an opportunity to advance practical arrangements for the fund, designed to support fair and equitable benefit-sharing from commercial use of digital sequence information on genetic resources.

Tracking progress: Better monitoring, data, capacity and cooperation are needed so countries can measure whether commitments are actually delivering results.

Changing the economics: Some of the areas furthest behind require action outside environment ministries, including on finance, business, sustainable consumption and harmful incentives.

© Unsplash/Jack5parrow

Yerevan’s test

For host Armenia, success means COP17 becoming both a “review COP” and an “implementation COP”.

“We cannot treat 2030 as a distant deadline,” Ambassador Hovhannisyan told UN News. “Decisions taken in Yerevan must help close the gap between commitments and results on the ground.”

Hambardzum Matevosyan, Armenia’s Environment Minister and incoming COP17 president, puts the progression simply: COP15 produced the framework and COP16 advanced mechanisms to implement it. COP17, he said, must establish “where we stand, what is working, where progress is falling short and what must change”.

The bottom line

Biodiversity can sound abstract. Its loss is anything but.

As António Guterres reminded leaders on Friday, the food we eat, the water we drink and the air we breathe depend on it. The question in Yerevan is whether countries can turn an ambitious global agreement into action quickly enough.

On Thursday, launching a major UN report evaluating global progress under the landmark Kunming framework, Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity, distilled the challenge: “We know where we stand. We know where the gaps are. Now, we must work together to close them.”

articles.personality_title: COP17 meets in Armenia to speed up global efforts to save nature
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The world agreed in 2022 on a plan called the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. This plan sets goals to stop and reverse damage to nature by 2030. Countries promised to protect land and sea, fight pollution, and support wildlife. Now, at COP17 in Yerevan, Armenia, leaders are checking how well they are doing halfway to the 2030 deadline.

**What happened** – From October 19 to 30, 2023, governments are meeting to review progress on the biodiversity goals. Almost all countries have set national targets and many have made plans to protect nature. But less than half of these targets are on track. The meeting focuses on finding ways to turn promises into real action, including raising money and improving how progress is measured.

**Impact** – This meeting is important because it moves the global effort from ideas to results. Protecting nature affects the food we eat, the water we drink, and the air we breathe. The discussions will decide how to close gaps in funding, cooperation, and data. It also aims to make sure that countries not only set goals but actually achieve them on the ground.

**What's next step** – COP17 will produce a clear report on where countries stand and what needs to change. It will work on practical plans to fund biodiversity projects and improve how progress is tracked. The next four years are crucial to reach the 2030 targets and avoid further harm to nature.

**One-sentence takeaway** – COP17 is a key moment for countries to turn their nature protection promises into real actions before 2030.
articles.personality_title_fr: La COP17 en Arménie pour accélérer la protection de la nature dans le monde
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En 2022, le monde a adopté un plan appelé le Cadre mondial pour la biodiversité de Kunming-Montréal. Ce plan fixe des objectifs pour arrêter et inverser les dégâts causés à la nature d’ici 2030. Les pays se sont engagés à protéger les terres et les mers, lutter contre la pollution et soutenir la faune. À la COP17 à Erevan, en Arménie, les dirigeants évaluent où ils en sont à mi-chemin de cet objectif.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Du 19 au 30 octobre 2023, les gouvernements se réunissent pour faire le point sur les progrès réalisés. Presque tous les pays ont défini des objectifs nationaux et beaucoup ont mis en place des plans pour protéger la nature. Mais moins de la moitié de ces objectifs sont en bonne voie. La réunion vise à transformer les promesses en actions concrètes, notamment en trouvant des financements et en améliorant le suivi des progrès.

**Impact** – Cette réunion est importante car elle fait passer l’effort mondial des idées aux résultats. Protéger la nature influence notre nourriture, notre eau et notre air. Les discussions doivent combler les lacunes en financement, coopération et données. Il s’agit aussi de s’assurer que les pays atteignent réellement leurs objectifs sur le terrain.

**Prochaine étape** – La COP17 produira un rapport clair sur la situation des pays et ce qui doit changer. Elle travaillera sur des plans pratiques pour financer des projets de biodiversité et améliorer le suivi. Les quatre prochaines années seront cruciales pour atteindre les objectifs de 2030 et éviter de nouveaux dégâts à la nature.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – La COP17 est un moment clé pour que les pays transforment leurs promesses de protection de la nature en actions concrètes avant 2030.

articles.title: Turning the tides: Could hidden sea power energise our coastal towns?
articles.summary: Engineer David Mummery has developed a tidal energy generator that he says can change lives for people living in coastal communities.
articles.content:
In a secret location in the Highlands of Scotland, there's a fast-flowing river that's the key to understanding the massive power of water.

It's where engineer David Mummery found himself more than a decade ago.

With a length of cord tied tightly across the river, he swam out, gripped firmly, and let the unstoppable current rush over as he sunk his head below the surface.

"As an engineer we do the maths and stuff," he says, "but sometimes you can get a lot more from actually touching the water and feeling it".

As he lay down in the powerful rapids, he visualised a new type of small-scale tidal energy generator.

It's an innovation he says could change lives for people in coastal communities.

"I'd be under the river, feeling the turbulence of the water rushing over me.

"Trying to envisage how this turbine needed to interact with that environment - to understand the way the water was working."
articles.reasoning: The article describes an innovative tidal energy generator developed by an engineer that has the potential to provide sustainable energy to coastal communities, representing a meaningful advancement in renewable energy with broad environmental and social benefits.
articles.personality_title: New tidal energy device aims to power coastal towns sustainably
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Coastal communities often face challenges in accessing reliable and clean energy. Harnessing the power of tides, which flow in and out with the ocean, offers a promising source of renewable energy.

**What happened** – Engineer David Mummery spent over ten years studying fast-moving water in a river in the Scottish Highlands. By physically experiencing the strong currents, he designed a new small-scale tidal energy generator that can efficiently capture energy from flowing water.

**Impact** – This tidal generator could provide clean electricity to towns near the sea, reducing their reliance on fossil fuels. Its small size means it can be installed in various locations without harming the environment. This innovation offers a fresh way to use natural water movement for practical energy needs.

**What's next step** – The next phase involves testing the generator in real coastal waters and working with communities to install it where it can help most. If successful, it could lead to wider use of this technology in other coastal areas around the world.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new tidal energy device created by an engineer in Scotland could bring clean, reliable power to coastal towns by using the natural flow of water.
articles.personality_title_fr: Un nouveau dispositif marémoteur pour alimenter durablement les villes côtières

**Contexte** – Les communautés côtières rencontrent souvent des difficultés à accéder à une énergie propre et fiable. Exploiter la puissance des marées, qui montent et descendent avec l'océan, offre une source prometteuse d'énergie renouvelable.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – L'ingénieur David Mummery a passé plus de dix ans à étudier le courant rapide d'une rivière dans les Highlands écossais. En ressentant physiquement la force du courant, il a conçu un nouveau générateur d'énergie marémotrice à petite échelle capable de capter efficacement l'énergie de l'eau en mouvement.

**Impact** – Ce générateur marémoteur pourrait fournir de l'électricité propre aux villes situées près de la mer, réduisant leur dépendance aux combustibles fossiles. Sa petite taille permet de l'installer à divers endroits sans nuire à l'environnement. Cette innovation offre une nouvelle façon d'utiliser le mouvement naturel de l'eau pour répondre aux besoins énergétiques.

**Prochaine étape** – La prochaine phase consiste à tester le générateur en milieu côtier réel et à collaborer avec les communautés pour l'installer là où il sera le plus utile. En cas de succès, cette technologie pourrait être déployée dans d'autres zones côtières dans le monde.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Un nouveau dispositif marémoteur créé par un ingénieur en Écosse pourrait apporter une énergie propre et fiable aux villes côtières en utilisant le mouvement naturel de l'eau.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo dispositivo de energía mareomotriz para alimentar sosteniblemente a ciudades costeras
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las comunidades costeras a menudo enfrentan dificultades para acceder a energía limpia y confiable. Aprovechar la fuerza de las mareas, que suben y bajan con el océano, ofrece una fuente prometedora de energía renovable.

**Qué pasó** – El ingeniero David Mummery pasó más de diez años estudiando el agua rápida de un río en las Tierras Altas de Escocia. Al sentir físicamente la fuerza de la corriente, diseñó un nuevo generador de energía mareomotriz a pequeña escala que puede capturar energía del agua en movimiento de manera eficiente.

**Impacto** – Este generador mareomotriz podría proporcionar electricidad limpia a ciudades cercanas al mar, reduciendo su dependencia de combustibles fósiles. Su tamaño pequeño permite instalarlo en varios lugares sin dañar el medio ambiente. Esta innovación ofrece una nueva forma de usar el movimiento natural del agua para necesidades energéticas prácticas.

**Próximo paso** – La siguiente fase es probar el generador en aguas costeras reales y trabajar con las comunidades para instalarlo donde más se necesite. Si tiene éxito, podría usarse en otras áreas costeras del mundo.

**Resumen en una frase** – Un nuevo dispositivo mareomotriz creado por un ingeniero en Escocia podría traer energía limpia y confiable a las ciudades costeras usando el flujo natural del agua.

articles.title: Seal pups spotted at nature reserve for 12th year
articles.summary: Two pups have been recorded at South Walney, home to Cumbria's only breeding grey seal colony.
articles.content:
Seal pups have been recorded at a nature reserve for the 12th year running.

Cumbria Wildlife Trust confirmed two pups had been spotted at South Walney Nature Reserve near Barrow, Cumbria.

The reserve is home to the county's only breeding grey seal colony and major haul-out site, a spot where seals come to shore for rest.

A record number of 14 seal pups were counted at the nature reserve last year, with the trust saying it hoped there would be "many more to come".

The pups were the first two healthy ones spotted at the nature reserve this season during a routine seal count.

Two were seen earlier in the summer but did not survive, the trust said.

Marine conservation officer Beth Churn said: "This is always an exciting time of year for us, and we hope that there'll be many more to come.

"We regularly reach double figures of pups, a trend that's been improving each year, so let's hope this season is a successful one for the colony."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a positive and ongoing trend of grey seal pup births at a nature reserve, indicating successful conservation efforts and a healthy marine ecosystem. The story has significance for wildlife conservation and the environment, with clear context and details about the breeding colony's status over multiple years.
articles.personality_title: Seal pups spotted again at Cumbria nature reserve for 12th year
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – South Walney Nature Reserve in Cumbria is home to the county’s only breeding grey seal colony. Each year, seals come ashore here to rest and give birth to pups.

**What happened** – For the 12th year in a row, seal pups have been seen at South Walney. This year, two healthy pups were recorded during a routine count. Earlier in the summer, two other pups were spotted but unfortunately did not survive.

**Impact** – The steady number of seal pups shows that the grey seal colony is doing well. Last year, a record 14 pups were counted, and the numbers have been growing over time. This is a sign that the seals are thriving in their protected environment.

**What's next step** – Conservation teams will continue to monitor the seal population throughout the season. They hope to see more pups born and grow strong, helping the colony to keep growing.

**One-sentence takeaway** – For 12 years, South Walney Nature Reserve has supported a growing grey seal colony, with new pups spotted again this season.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Pour la 12e année de suite, des bébés phoques ont été observés à South Walney. Cette année, deux petits en bonne santé ont été comptés lors d’un dénombrement régulier. Deux autres avaient été vus plus tôt cet été, mais n’ont pas survécu.

**Impact** – Le nombre stable de bébés phoques montre que la colonie de phoques gris se porte bien. L’année dernière, un record de 14 petits avait été compté, et les chiffres augmentent avec le temps. Cela indique que les phoques prospèrent dans leur environnement protégé.

**Prochaine étape** – Les équipes de conservation continueront à surveiller la population de phoques pendant la saison. Elles espèrent voir naître et grandir davantage de petits pour aider la colonie à se développer.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Depuis 12 ans, la réserve naturelle de South Walney soutient une colonie croissante de phoques gris, avec de nouveaux petits aperçus cette saison.
articles.personality_title_es: Cachorros de foca avistados nuevamente en reserva natural de Cumbria por 12º año
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La reserva natural South Walney en Cumbria es hogar de la única colonia de focas grises que se reproducen en el condado. Cada año, las focas llegan a la orilla para descansar y tener a sus crías.

**Qué pasó** – Por 12º año consecutivo, se han visto cachorros de foca en South Walney. Este año, se registraron dos cachorros sanos durante un conteo rutinario. A principios del verano, se vieron dos cachorros más, pero no sobrevivieron.

**Impacto** – El número constante de cachorros muestra que la colonia de focas grises está bien. El año pasado se contó un récord de 14 cachorros, y la cantidad ha ido aumentando con el tiempo. Esto indica que las focas prosperan en su entorno protegido.

**Próximo paso** – Los equipos de conservación seguirán monitoreando la población de focas durante la temporada. Esperan ver más cachorros nacer y crecer para ayudar a que la colonia siga creciendo.

**Frase clave** – Durante 12 años, la reserva natural South Walney ha apoyado una colonia creciente de focas grises, con nuevos cachorros avistados nuevamente esta temporada.
